lessons.title: The Roaring Twenties and Republican prosperity
lessons.description: Mass production, consumer credit and the boom that wasn't shared by all Americans.
lessons.content_html:
America After the First World War

When Warren Harding won the presidential election of 1920 on a promise of a “return to normalcy,” he captured a national mood. Americans were tired of wartime controls, high taxes, and international entanglements. The decade that followed — the 1920s — brought extraordinary economic growth for millions, but that prosperity was deeply uneven. Understanding who gained and who did not is essential for this unit.

Key Fact

Three Republican administrations — Harding (1921–23), Coolidge (1923–29), and Hoover (1929) — followed a broadly laissez-faire approach. Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon cut income taxes sharply through the 1921 and 1924 Revenue Acts, on the theory that wealthy investors would reinvest their savings in industry. High tariffs — the Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1921 — protected American manufacturers from foreign competition.

The Assembly Line and Consumer Society

The technological engine of the boom was mass production, perfected by Henry Ford at his Highland Park plant. Ford’s moving assembly line slashed the time needed to build a Model T from over twelve hours to roughly ninety minutes. By 1929, US car production had reached approximately 5.6 million vehicles a year. The car in turn stimulated steel, glass, rubber, and oil industries, and accelerated the growth of road-building and suburban development.

Americans were also buying on credit in unprecedented numbers. Hire-purchase agreements allowed families to acquire radios, refrigerators, washing machines, and vacuum cleaners before they had saved the full purchase price. Advertising, a rapidly growing industry, shaped new desires and convinced consumers that prosperity was within reach. Radio stations multiplied — from one in 1921 to over 500 by 1923. Hollywood produced films that both reflected and promoted a culture of consumption.

The boom bypassed large parts of the American economy. Farmers were among the hardest hit. During the First World War, US agriculture had expanded rapidly to feed Europe. Once European farms recovered after 1918, demand fell sharply while production remained high, pushing prices down. Farmers who had borrowed to buy land and equipment during the war years faced foreclosure. Rural poverty was widespread throughout the 1920s — long before the Great Depression began.

Coal miners, textile workers in the South, and workers in older industries such as leather goods and shipbuilding also saw stagnant wages or declining employment. Trade union membership fell sharply across the decade as employers used court injunctions, the threat of replacement workers (often called “scabs”), and company unions to undermine collective bargaining. Women in domestic service and garment work, and African American workers across most of the country, were largely excluded from the prosperity the decade is famous for.

Republican Ideology and Its Limits

Republican presidents of the 1920s believed firmly that government should not interfere with business. Coolidge famously remarked that “the chief business of the American people is business.” This philosophy translated into low business taxes, limited regulation of financial markets, and the freedom for companies to set their own terms. The Mellon tax cuts disproportionately benefited high earners: the top rate of income tax fell from 73 per cent in 1921 to 25 per cent by 1925.

This approach had a structural weakness that was not fully understood at the time. Wages for ordinary workers did not rise fast enough to absorb all the goods the new factories were producing. Much of the consumer spending of the 1920s was financed by credit. Equally dangerous was the growth of buying stocks on margin. By 1929, share prices had risen far above the value of the underlying companies. When confidence broke, the crash would be catastrophic.

Key Fact

The prosperity of the 1920s excluded several large groups: farmers facing falling crop prices; coal and textile workers in declining industries; African Americans, who faced segregation and discrimination across most of the country; recent immigrants in low-wage factory jobs; and the roughly 40 per cent of Americans living in poverty throughout the decade according to contemporary surveys.

Herbert Hoover, elected president in November 1928 over Democrat Al Smith, was widely regarded as one of the most competent men in American public life. He had successfully directed food relief for millions in Europe after the First World War, and as Secretary of Commerce from 1921 to 1928, he had actively promoted business efficiency and trade associations. His election on a platform of continuing Republican prosperity seemed to mark a high point of confidence. Within a year, the Wall Street Crash would transform his presidency entirely.

The Harlem Renaissance

One of the most significant cultural developments of the decade took place largely outside the mainstream economy of the boom. The Harlem Renaissance saw African American writers, musicians, and artists produce work of lasting importance — from Langston Hughes’s poetry to Louis Armstrong’s jazz. The Great Migration, in which hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved from the rural South to northern cities between roughly 1910 and 1930, created a critical mass of Black urban communities. Yet racial discrimination, enforced by Jim Crow laws in the South and informal segregation in the North, meant the majority of African Americans remained trapped in low-paid, insecure employment regardless of this cultural flourishing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on the Roaring Twenties often ask you to explain why not everyone prospered. Avoid giving a one-sided answer that treats the decade as simply a time of boom. Always identify at least two groups that were excluded — farmers and African Americans are the strongest examples — and explain the specific reasons for their exclusion (falling crop prices for farmers; segregation and job discrimination for African Americans). For essay questions asking you to weigh how far Republican policies caused the prosperity, make sure you discuss both the policies themselves (tariffs, tax cuts, laissez-faire) and the role of new technology (assembly line, consumer credit) to show a range of causal factors.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Republican administrations of the 1920s followed a laissez-faire approach — low taxes, high tariffs, and minimal regulation — which helped fuel economic growth for some Americans but left farmers, African Americans, and workers in declining industries behind.
  • Mass production (Ford’s assembly line), consumer credit, and rising share prices drove the surface prosperity of the decade, but wages did not keep pace with output and speculation on the stock market created hidden instability.
  • The boom was highly unequal: roughly 40 per cent of Americans lived in poverty throughout the 1920s, and the Harlem Renaissance flourished alongside persistent racial discrimination in employment and housing.

practice_questions.text: Outline two features of Republican economic policy in the 1920s.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each feature scores 1 mark for identification and 1 additional mark for specific supporting detail. Example features: laissez-faire approach (1) meaning minimal government interference in business, so companies could set their own wages and resist regulation (1); Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1921 (1) raised duties on imported goods to protect American manufacturers from foreign competition (1); Mellon tax cuts (1) reduced the top rate of income tax from 73 per cent to 25 per cent to encourage investment (1). Maximum 5 marks from any combination.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why farmers did not share in the prosperity of the Roaring Twenties.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence and clear causal analysis (e.g. wartime overexpansion meant US farms had borrowed heavily to increase production, but when European agriculture recovered after 1918 demand fell sharply, leaving farmers unable to repay debts; trade union weakness and the prevalence of sharecropping also kept farm incomes low). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both reasons identified but not explained with causal link.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the prosperity of the 1920s was built on unstable foundations.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies and explains at least two structural weaknesses — consumer spending financed by credit rather than rising wages, and share speculation on margin; links both to the eventual collapse in 1929. May also mention overproduction in agriculture and the uneven distribution of wealth. Secure: Two factors explained with relevant evidence and causal link to instability. Developing: One factor explained, others named. Emerging: General statement about problems without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Henry Ford's assembly line production methods.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Workers performed one specialised task repeatedly (1); this reduced the time to build a Model T from over twelve hours to roughly ninety minutes (1). Feature 2: The production line moved continuously, bringing components to the worker (1); this allowed Ford to produce approximately 5.6 million vehicles a year by 1929 (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the prosperity of the 1920s was the result of Republican government policies? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained, balanced argument that acknowledges the role of Republican policies (Mellon tax cuts, Fordney-McCumber Tariff, laissez-faire regulation) while also crediting technological change (Ford assembly line, electrification), consumer credit, and American natural resources; uses specific evidence throughout; engages with at least one interpretation. Secure: Clear argument addressing both the role of policy and other factors, with relevant evidence from the decade. Developing: Some awareness of multiple causes with basic evidence; may be one-sided. Emerging: Descriptive account of the boom without structured argument. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of the Roaring Twenties. Interpretation A argues the decade was a genuine economic revolution that raised living standards for most Americans. Interpretation B argues the prosperity was superficial and excluded millions. How far do the interpretations differ, and what might explain their differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies key points of difference (who benefited, the role of credit, agricultural poverty); uses own knowledge to evaluate both (e.g. rising car ownership and appliance sales support A; farm foreclosures, African American poverty, and falling union membership support B); explains why interpretations differ (different evidence base, different focus on sectors). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Identifies some differences and supports one interpretation. Emerging: Summarises each interpretation without explaining differences.

lessons.title: Women, the Sheppard-Towner Act and the 19th Amendment
lessons.description: Suffrage won but limited — what the 19th Amendment changed and what it left untouched.
lessons.content_html:
Women and the Vote

In August 1920, the 19th Amendment was ratified, completing a campaign for women’s suffrage that had been active since the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848. The amendment stated that the right to vote could not be denied on account of sex. It was a landmark achievement, but its practical impact was more limited than its supporters had hoped — and for Black women in the South, it changed almost nothing.

Key Fact

The 19th Amendment gave women the legal right to vote in federal and state elections from 1920. However, in the southern states, Jim Crow voter suppression tactics — literacy tests, poll taxes, and outright intimidation — that were used to prevent African American men from voting applied equally to African American women. White women in the South voted in significant numbers; Black women largely could not.

The Sheppard-Towner Act

The most significant piece of federal legislation directly connected to women’s political power in this period was the Sheppard-Towner Maternity Act, signed into law in November 1921. The act provided federal grants to states to establish prenatal and child welfare clinics. Women’s organisations, particularly the newly formed League of Women Voters, had lobbied hard for it, and many congressmen feared the consequences of opposing women’s welfare issues so soon after the 19th Amendment.

The Sheppard-Towner Act was genuinely significant: it created over 3,000 child health centres across the country, and infant mortality rates fell in states that participated. However, it was strongly opposed by the American Medical Association, which saw it as government interference in medicine, and by conservatives who feared it as a step towards socialism. Funding was repeatedly contested, and the act was allowed to expire in 1929 without renewal.

After the 19th Amendment, the suffrage movement split over strategy. The League of Women Voters, led by Carrie Chapman Catt, focused on educating women voters and working within the existing party system. Alice Paul’s National Woman’s Party took a more radical approach, introducing the Equal Rights Amendment in 1923 — a proposed constitutional amendment that would prohibit all sex-based discrimination. The ERA was repeatedly blocked in Congress through the 1920s; it was not passed until 1972, and even then it failed ratification.

Florence Kelley of the National Consumers League argued that the ERA would actually harm women workers by removing the protective labour legislation (such as limits on night shifts and maximum hours) that reformers had fought for. This tension between formal legal equality and protective special legislation divided women’s organisations throughout the 1920s and beyond.

Flappers and Changing Social Norms

The 1920s saw visible changes in women’s public behaviour, associated most strongly with the figure of the flapper. Young, urban, middle-class women cut their hair short, wore shorter skirts, danced at jazz clubs, and smoked in public. These visible changes shocked conservative opinion and suggested a broader loosening of Victorian social norms.

However, historians caution against overstating the significance of flapper culture. It was largely confined to urban, white, middle-class women. Most women — rural, working-class, or African American — saw little change in their economic position or their domestic expectations. Women workers remained concentrated in low-paid sectors: domestic service, garment manufacture, and clerical work. Married women faced widespread social pressure and often legal barriers to remaining in paid employment.

Key Fact

The Sheppard-Towner Maternity Act of 1921 was the first federal welfare law specifically aimed at women and children. It funded state child health clinics and reduced infant mortality where it operated. Opposition from the American Medical Association and conservative politicians, who saw it as “socialist,” led to its expiry in 1929 when Congress refused to renew funding.

Despite the vote and the Sheppard-Towner Act, much remained unchanged. Women were still largely excluded from professional careers in law and medicine by informal discrimination. The Equal Rights Amendment failed to pass, so legal inequalities in employment and property rights remained. African American women in the South were effectively denied the vote by Jim Crow measures. And the cultural freedoms of flapper culture were always limited to a minority — most American women in the 1920s were wives and mothers in rural or small-town environments where expectations had changed little.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on women in the 1920s often require you to assess change and continuity. Avoid treating the 19th Amendment as a straightforward success story. The strongest answers will acknowledge the genuine significance of the vote and the Sheppard-Towner Act, while also explaining the limits of change — Jim Crow denial of the vote to Black women, the ERA’s failure, and the persistence of employment discrimination. When describing flappers, make sure you contextualise them as a minority experience rather than a universal change.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 19th Amendment (1920) gave women the legal right to vote, but Jim Crow voter suppression in the South meant that African American women were effectively denied this right in practice.
  • The Sheppard-Towner Act (1921) was a significant welfare achievement lobbied for by women’s organisations, but it expired in 1929 due to opposition from the medical establishment and conservatives.
  • The ERA, first introduced in 1923 by Alice Paul, and the social changes associated with flappers showed the aspirations of the era, but most American women — especially rural, working-class, and Black women — experienced limited practical change during the 1920s.

lessons.title: Prohibition: causes, enforcement and failure
lessons.description: How the Volstead Act tried to dry out America — and what bootleggers and speakeasies did with it.
lessons.content_html:
America Goes Dry

On 17 January 1920, the Prohibition came into force across the United States. The 18th Amendment to the Constitution, ratified in January 1919, had banned the production, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors. The Volstead Act, passed in October 1919, defined the legal threshold (anything over 0.5 per cent alcohol) and gave enforcement powers to federal agents. The ambition was sweeping: to eliminate drunkenness, domestic violence, poverty, and crime by removing alcohol from American life. The reality was very different.

Key Fact

Prohibition grew from three overlapping movements: the Protestant temperance movement, which had campaigned for decades against drinking as a moral evil; the Progressive reformers, who argued that alcohol was the root cause of urban poverty and domestic abuse; and a strand of nativism, which associated alcohol with German beer halls and southern European wine-drinking immigrants. The Anti-Saloon League, led by Wayne Wheeler, co-ordinated this coalition and was the most effective single-issue pressure group in American history to that point.

Enforcement and Its Failures

From the outset, Prohibition was extraordinarily difficult to enforce. The Volstead Act created a federal Prohibition Bureau, but it was chronically underfunded and its agents were notoriously susceptible to bribery. In 1920, there were only about 1,500 agents covering the entire country. Large sections of the American public — particularly in cities, among immigrant communities, and in wealthier social circles — had no intention of stopping drinking.

Illegal drinking establishments, known as speakeasies, multiplied across American cities. New York City, which had roughly 15,000 legal bars before Prohibition, was estimated to have between 20,000 and 30,000 speakeasies by the late 1920s. Bootleggers supplied them through a combination of domestic illegal distillation, smuggling from Canada and the Caribbean, and the diversion of industrial alcohol.

Key Fact

Al Capone’s organisation in Chicago demonstrated how far Prohibition had failed. By the late 1920s, Capone’s criminal network was earning an estimated $60 million a year from bootlegging, gambling, and other illegal activities. He employed hundreds of people and had bribed significant numbers of police officers and city officials. The St Valentine’s Day Massacre of February 1929, in which seven members of a rival gang were shot dead, showed the murderous competition for control of bootlegging territory. Capone was eventually convicted — not for bootlegging but for tax evasion — in 1931.

Prohibition accelerated the growth of organised crime in American cities. Criminal networks that had previously focused on gambling and prostitution expanded massively into the alcohol trade, using violence to enforce territory and corruption to neutralise law enforcement. Federal agent Eliot Ness and his team, nicknamed the “Untouchables” for their refusal to take bribes, became famous for their raids on Capone’s breweries — but their victories were largely tactical rather than strategic. The Capone organisation survived and adapted repeatedly.

Corruption was not limited to Chicago. In major cities across the country, Prohibition created a system in which police, judges, and politicians accepted payment to allow the illegal trade to operate. This widespread corruption damaged public respect for law enforcement and the legal system more broadly, contributing to the eventual political momentum for repeal.

The Road to Repeal

Support for Prohibition weakened through the late 1920s and collapsed during the Great Depression. The economic argument shifted decisively: a legal alcohol industry would generate tax revenue and jobs at precisely the moment the government needed both. The Association Against the Prohibition Amendment, funded by wealthy industrialists, lobbied effectively for repeal. Franklin Roosevelt, who supported repeal, won the 1932 election in a landslide. The 21st Amendment, ratified in December 1933, ended Prohibition — the only time a constitutional amendment has been repealed in American history.

Historians note that Prohibition was not a total failure. Alcohol consumption did fall significantly in the early years of Prohibition — cirrhosis death rates dropped, arrests for public drunkenness declined, and there is evidence of reduced domestic violence in some areas. But these gains were largely reversed as the bootlegging economy grew. By the mid-1920s, drinking was widespread again, concentrated in cities and among the middle class. The rural Protestant communities that had driven Prohibition remained broadly supportive throughout, while urban, immigrant, and working-class communities rejected it consistently.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on Prohibition often ask you to explain its failure. Make sure you address multiple causes rather than focusing only on Al Capone. Strong answers will discuss: the inadequacy of enforcement (too few agents, widespread bribery); the lack of public support in cities and among immigrant communities; the growth of organised crime; and the economic arguments that strengthened during the Depression. The repeal in 1933 is itself evidence of failure — use the 21st Amendment as a specific piece of evidence for your conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Prohibition (1920–1933) was driven by the temperance movement, Progressive reformers, and nativist sentiment, co-ordinated by the Anti-Saloon League under Wayne Wheeler.
  • Enforcement was chronically underfunded and corrupt; speakeasies multiplied and Al Capone’s criminal network earned an estimated $60 million a year from bootlegging, demonstrating the scale of non-compliance.
  • The 21st Amendment repealed Prohibition in December 1933 — the only constitutional amendment ever to repeal a previous one — as economic arguments for tax revenue and jobs combined with widespread public rejection of the law.

lessons.title: Jim Crow, the Klan and racial violence
lessons.description: Segregation in law, lynchings in practice and the Klan's 1920s revival — racial backlash exposed.
lessons.content_html:
Jim Crow America

Throughout the 1920s, the majority of African Americans lived under a system of legal and social oppression enforced across the South and, in different forms, throughout much of the country. The Jim Crow laws mandated separation of the races in schools, transport, restaurants, hospitals, and public spaces. The Supreme Court’s 1896 ruling in Plessy v Ferguson had declared “separate but equal” facilities constitutional — in practice, Black facilities were always inferior and the equality was fiction.

Key Fact

Jim Crow laws in the South denied African Americans equal access to education, barred them from voting through literacy tests, poll taxes, and grandfather clauses, prohibited interracial marriage, and enforced segregation in virtually all public spaces. Employment discrimination kept most Black workers in the lowest-paid, most insecure jobs regardless of their qualifications. The economic consequences were reinforced by physical terror: according to records maintained by the Tuskegee Institute, 3,446 Black Americans were lynched between 1882 and 1968, with the highest rates in the period before and after the First World War.

The Klan’s Second Revival

The original Ku Klux Klan had been suppressed in the 1870s. In 1915, a new organisation calling itself the Ku Klux Klan was refounded at Stone Mountain, Georgia, partly inspired by D.W. Griffith’s film The Birth of a Nation (1915), which portrayed the original Klan as heroic. This second Klan was broader in scope than its predecessor: it targeted not only African Americans but also Catholics, Jews, immigrants, and anyone it characterised as morally degenerate.

The Klan grew explosively in the early 1920s. By 1924 to 1925, membership had reached an estimated 4 to 6 million, with significant strength outside the South — in Indiana, Ohio, and Oregon as well as the traditional strongholds of the former Confederacy. Indiana Grand Dragon D.C. Stephenson built a powerful political machine that influenced state government and claimed to have elected congressmen and a governor.

The most devastating single act of racial violence in the 1920s occurred in Tulsa, Oklahoma, in May–June 1921. Greenwood, a prosperous African American neighbourhood known as “Black Wall Street,” was attacked by a white mob that included some deputised civilians. Homes and businesses were burned, and aircraft may have been used to fire on the neighbourhood. The 2001 Oklahoma Commission, established to investigate the events, concluded that at least 36 people died (other estimates are substantially higher) and roughly 35 blocks of Greenwood were destroyed. The event had been largely suppressed from public memory for decades. Tulsa city government officially adopted the term “massacre” in 2001 — use this framing rather than the older term “riot,” which implies mutual combat rather than an organised attack on a community.

Red Summer 1919 and the Context of Violence

The racial violence of the 1920s did not emerge from nowhere. The summer of 1919 — known as the Red Summer — saw race riots in at least 25 American cities, including Chicago and Washington DC. African American soldiers who had served in France came home expecting greater respect and rights; they encountered instead intensified racial hostility. The NAACP, led by James Weldon Johnson and W.E.B. Du Bois, documented and publicised these outrages, campaigning for a federal anti-lynching law. Every such bill was filibustered to death in the Senate by Southern politicians through the entire period covered by this unit.

Key Fact

The Klan’s membership collapsed after 1925 for several reasons. D.C. Stephenson, the Indiana Grand Dragon, was convicted of rape and second-degree murder in 1925 after the death of a woman he had assaulted on a train. His conviction destroyed the Klan’s claim to stand for moral decency. Press exposure of corruption among Klan-affiliated politicians, and internal factional fighting, accelerated the decline. By the late 1920s, membership had fallen from millions to a few hundred thousand.

African Americans responded to racial violence and oppression in multiple ways. The NAACP, led by W.E.B. Du Bois (who edited its magazine The Crisis) and James Weldon Johnson, pursued legal and political strategies. Marcus Garvey’s Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) offered a different vision: Black economic self-sufficiency and ultimately a return to Africa, encapsulated in his “Back to Africa” movement. At its peak in the early 1920s, the UNIA had claimed several million members worldwide, though these figures were disputed. The Great Migration, in which around 1.6 million African Americans moved from the South to northern cities between 1910 and 1930, was itself a form of resistance — leaving the most oppressive conditions — though discrimination followed them North.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on racial violence and the Klan require you to apply impartiality: present the Klan’s revival as a historical reality without either sensationalising or minimising it. Frame the Klan as a product of specific historical conditions — post-war anxiety, nativism, and the threat white supremacists perceived from African American migration and assertion. Always use “Tulsa Race Massacre” (not “riot”). When answering questions about African American responses, distinguish between the NAACP’s legal/political approach, Garvey’s nationalist separatism, and the Great Migration as an economic response — examiners reward students who show multiple strategies.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jim Crow laws imposed legal segregation across the South, with lynching as physical terror: the Tuskegee Institute records 3,446 Black Americans lynched between 1882 and 1968.
  • The second Ku Klux Klan, refounded in 1915, reached 4–6 million members by the mid-1920s, extending far beyond the South and targeting Catholics, Jews, and immigrants as well as African Americans, before collapsing after the Stephenson scandal of 1925.
  • African Americans responded through the NAACP’s legal strategies, Garvey’s UNIA movement, and the Great Migration, but anti-lynching bills were repeatedly filibustered and formal equality remained entirely out of reach.

lessons.title: Immigration, the Red Scare and nativism
lessons.description: Palmer Raids, Sacco and Vanzetti, the National Origins Act — how 1920s America closed its doors.
lessons.content_html:
Fear of Radicals: The Red Scare

In the aftermath of the First World War and the Bolshevik Revolution in Russia, a wave of anxiety about Communist and anarchist subversion swept the United States. In 1919, a series of mail bombs targeting government officials — including a device sent to Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer — and a bomb explosion outside Palmer’s home in June 1919 intensified demands for action against radicals. The result was one of the most significant attacks on civil liberties in American peacetime history.

Key Fact

The Palmer Raids took place in two main waves: November 1919 and January 1920. In the January raids alone, around 10,000 people were arrested across 33 cities. Many were held for days without charges. Evidence was often minimal or fabricated. Several hundred people, mostly foreign-born, were deported to the Soviet Union. The head of the Bureau of Investigation’s General Intelligence Division, J. Edgar Hoover, compiled files on thousands of suspected radicals. He would go on to lead the FBI for the next five decades.

The Sacco and Vanzetti Case

In April 1920, two Italian-born anarchists, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, were arrested for the murder of a paymaster and his guard during a robbery in South Braintree, Massachusetts. Their trial in 1921 became a cause célèbre. Critics argued that the prosecution was driven by their immigrant background and political beliefs rather than the evidence. The judge, Webster Thayer, made comments about the defendants’ politics that suggested prejudice.

Despite international protests — demonstrations were held in Europe, South America, and across the United States — both men were executed on 23 August 1927. In 1977, Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis issued a proclamation declaring that Sacco and Vanzetti had been unfairly tried and condemning the atmosphere of prejudice that had surrounded the case. Their guilt has been debated for a century: ballistics evidence later analysed in the 1980s suggested Sacco’s gun may have been used, while Vanzetti’s guilt appears even less certain. Present their case as procedurally flawed rather than asserting innocence as established fact.

A more permanent expression of nativist sentiment was the National Origins Act of 1924, also known as the Johnson-Reed Act. It set immigration quotas at 2 per cent of each nationality’s presence in the 1890 census — a year chosen deliberately because it pre-dated the mass immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe. The effect was to sharply reduce immigration from Italy, Poland, Russia, and other countries, while largely preserving immigration from Britain and Western Europe. Immigration from Asian countries was effectively banned entirely. The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 had already begun this process; the 1924 act made it permanent and stricter.

Responses: NAACP and UNIA

The spec for this lesson also requires knowledge of attempts to combat prejudice. The NAACP, led by James Weldon Johnson as executive secretary from 1920 to 1930, campaigned tirelessly for federal anti-lynching legislation and challenged segregation through the courts. Its magazine The Crisis, edited by W.E.B. Du Bois, reached a circulation of around 100,000 by the early 1920s, documenting racial violence and intellectual Black life.

Key Fact

Marcus Garvey’s UNIA offered a separatist vision: Black economic self-sufficiency, pride in African heritage, and ultimately the creation of an independent Black nation in Africa. Garvey’s movement attracted millions of followers in the early 1920s, particularly among working-class African Americans in northern cities. Du Bois and the NAACP were deeply critical of Garvey’s separatism, which they saw as accepting rather than challenging racial inequality. Garvey was convicted of mail fraud in 1925 and deported to Jamaica in 1927, ending his American movement.

The Palmer Raids were eventually halted by a combination of legal challenges and political embarrassment. Assistant Secretary of Labor Louis Post cancelled thousands of deportation orders on due-process grounds. By 1920, Palmer’s prediction of a major Communist revolution on May Day had proved completely wrong, damaging his credibility. The American Civil Liberties Union, founded in 1920, emerged partly in response to the abuses of the Palmer era and would go on to challenge repressive laws throughout the decade. Palmer’s hoped-for presidential run in 1920 came to nothing.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This lesson covers several distinct topics that the exam may ask about separately. When writing about Sacco and Vanzetti, always emphasise the procedural flaws (judge’s comments, climate of anti-immigrant prejudice) rather than stating they were innocent — their guilt remains debated. For the National Origins Act, make sure you know the 1924 act used the 1890 census deliberately to exclude Southern and Eastern European immigrants — that specific detail shows you understand the act’s discriminatory design. On the NAACP vs. UNIA distinction, examiners reward answers that can explain the different strategies (legal integration vs. separatist nationalism) rather than simply naming both.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Palmer Raids of 1919–20 arrested around 10,000 people in a wave of anti-Communist and anti-anarchist repression, with J. Edgar Hoover compiling intelligence files that would shape his FBI career for five decades.
  • Sacco and Vanzetti’s trial and execution in 1927 became an international symbol of anti-immigrant prejudice and a flawed justice system; the case was officially condemned as unfair by Governor Dukakis in 1977.
  • The National Origins Act of 1924 used the 1890 census to drastically cut immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe and ban Asian immigration; the NAACP and UNIA offered contrasting strategies — legal integration and separatist nationalism — in response to continued racial discrimination.

lessons.title: The Great Depression and Hoover's response
lessons.description: Wall Street to bread lines — the 1929 crash, Hoovervilles and the limits of Hoover's response.
lessons.content_html:
The Wall Street Crash

On 24 October 1929 — Black Thursday — the New York Stock Exchange experienced catastrophic selling as investors tried to offload shares whose prices had been inflated far beyond the value of the underlying companies. A temporary rally followed when leading bankers pooled resources to buy shares and stabilise the market. It did not hold. On Tuesday 29 October — Black Tuesday — share prices collapsed entirely. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost around a quarter of its value in two days. By July 1932, it had fallen 89 per cent from its 1929 peak. It would not recover to pre-crash levels until 1954.

Key Fact

The crash was not caused by a single shock; it reflected structural weaknesses that had been building throughout the 1920s. Share speculation on buying on margin meant millions of investors owed money they could not repay when prices fell. Over-production in agriculture and industry meant companies were already earning less than their inflated share prices suggested. And consumer debt — the hire-purchase economy — left American families without the savings to sustain spending through a downturn.

The Great Depression: Scale and Human Cost

The Crash triggered a cascading economic crisis. Banks that had lent money for share speculation began to fail as borrowers defaulted. Between 1930 and 1933, roughly 9,000 American banks collapsed, wiping out the savings of millions of depositors. Without savings, families cut spending. Businesses responded by cutting production and sacking workers. Unemployment rose from around 3 per cent in 1929 to a peak of approximately 25 per cent by 1932 — around 13 to 15 million people out of work.

The human consequences were visible everywhere. Hoovervilles — shantytowns built from scrap wood, corrugated iron, and cardboard — appeared on the edges of cities and in parks. Bread lines and soup kitchens, many operated by charities and churches, fed hundreds of thousands. The Dust Bowl conditions in the Great Plains from the early 1930s drove hundreds of thousands of farming families off the land, the so-called “Okies” heading to California in search of work.

In June 1930, Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, raising taxes on over 20,000 imported goods to the highest levels in American history. The aim was to protect American industry and farmers from foreign competition. The result was a retaliatory tariff war: countries that exported to the US raised their own barriers, and American exports collapsed. World trade shrank by around 65 per cent between 1929 and 1934. The tariff is widely regarded by economic historians as having significantly deepened and prolonged the Depression.

Hoover’s Response: Neither Nothing Nor Enough

A common misconception among students is that Hoover “did nothing” in the face of the Depression. This is inaccurate, and examiners penalise oversimplification. Hoover did intervene: he convened conferences with business leaders and urged them voluntarily to maintain wages; he increased federal public works spending; and he created the RFC. But his interventions were constrained by his ideological commitment to voluntary co-operation and his deep reluctance to make the federal government directly responsible for individual welfare. At a time when 25 per cent unemployment required emergency action, ideological restraint proved catastrophic for millions of Americans and for Hoover’s presidency.

Key Fact

Hoover’s most significant economic intervention was the creation of the RFC (Reconstruction Finance Corporation) in January 1932, which lent money to banks and businesses at risk of failure. He also increased federal public works spending and encouraged states to create their own relief programmes. But he refused to authorise direct federal relief to unemployed individuals, believing this would create dependency and undermine personal character — a position that seemed increasingly out of touch as unemployment reached 25 per cent.

In July 1932, around 17,000 veterans of the First World War — the “Bonus Army” — marched on Washington DC demanding early payment of a war bonus Congress had promised for 1945. Hoover refused. When a confrontation with police resulted in deaths, he authorised General Douglas MacArthur to disperse the veterans. MacArthur exceeded his orders, using cavalry, tanks, and tear gas to drive the marchers, their wives, and children from their camps. Images of army units attacking their own veterans destroyed what remained of Hoover’s political standing. In November 1932, Franklin D. Roosevelt defeated Hoover in a landslide, winning 42 of 48 states. The Democratic era of American politics had begun.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Examiners consistently report that students describe Hoover as doing “nothing” about the Depression. This loses marks. You must show nuance: Hoover did act (RFC, public works, voluntary co-operation schemes), but his actions were inadequate because his ideology prevented him from authorising direct federal relief to individuals, and the Smoot-Hawley Tariff actively worsened the situation. The Bonus Army’s dispersal is an excellent piece of evidence for Hoover’s political failure. Always be specific about dates: the Crash is October 1929, peak unemployment was around 1932, and the election that ended Hoover’s presidency was November 1932.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Wall Street Crash of October 1929 (Black Thursday 24th, Black Tuesday 29th) was the trigger for the Great Depression — but its underlying causes lay in share speculation on margin, over-production, and consumer debt from the 1920s boom.
  • By 1932 unemployment had reached approximately 25 per cent; Hoovervilles, bread lines, and the Dust Bowl migration showed the human scale of the crisis.
  • Hoover did intervene (RFC, public works) but refused direct federal relief to individuals; the dispersal of the Bonus Army and the 1932 landslide election loss to Roosevelt sealed his political failure.

lessons.title: The First and Second New Deals
lessons.description: Hundred Days, Alphabet Agencies and the Wagner Act — Roosevelt remaking American government.
lessons.content_html:
Roosevelt Takes Office

Franklin D. Roosevelt was inaugurated as the 32nd President of the United States on 4 March 1933. In his famous opening address, he told the American people that “the only thing we have to fear is fear itself” — framing the Depression as a crisis of confidence that decisive action could break. Within the first hundred days of his presidency, he and Congress passed a remarkable series of laws that transformed the relationship between the federal government and the American economy. The scale of intervention was without peacetime precedent.

Key Fact

The Hundred Days (March–June 1933) produced the core of the First New Deal. Key agencies created included: the AAA (Agricultural Adjustment Agency), which paid farmers to reduce production in order to raise food prices; the CCC (Civilian Conservation Corps), which employed young men in national parks and forests; the FERA (Federal Emergency Relief Administration), which gave half a billion dollars in grants to states for direct relief; the NRA (National Recovery Administration), which set codes of fair competition across industries; and the TVA (Tennessee Valley Authority), which built dams and provided electricity to seven previously impoverished Southern states.

The Scale of Federal Expansion

The New Deal represented an unprecedented expansion of federal government. Before 1933, Washington spent a tiny fraction of national income and employed a small workforce. By 1936, federal spending had roughly doubled as a share of the economy. Millions of Americans experienced the federal government directly for the first time — through a CCC paycheck, a FERA relief cheque, or a TVA electricity connection in a home that had never had power. The Glass-Steagall Act (June 1933) separated commercial and investment banking and created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, guaranteeing bank deposits and halting the bank-run panics that had destroyed savings in 1930–33.

The Second New Deal

By 1935, the Supreme Court had declared the NRA unconstitutional in the Schechter Poultry case (May 1935) and the AAA was also struck down the following year. Roosevelt responded with a second wave of legislation in 1935 — often called the Second New Deal — that shifted emphasis from economic co-ordination to workers’ rights and social security.

The Wagner Act (National Labor Relations Act, 1935) guaranteed workers the right to join trade unions and bargain collectively with employers. It was the most important piece of labour legislation in American history to that point. The Social Security Act (August 1935) established old-age pensions for workers over 65 and a system of unemployment insurance — the first federal social safety net in American history. The Works Progress Administration (WPA), under Harry Hopkins, employed over 8 million people in building projects and arts programmes.

The New Deal was not a single person’s work. Frances Perkins, Roosevelt’s Labor Secretary and the first woman to serve in a US Cabinet, was the principal architect of the Social Security Act and the federal minimum wage. Harry Hopkins, who ran FERA and later the WPA, was Roosevelt’s closest adviser on relief policy and spent money on direct help faster and more effectively than Hoover had ever contemplated. Senator Robert Wagner of New York championed the labour rights act that bears his name against fierce business opposition. Eleanor Roosevelt pressed her husband to do more for African Americans, women workers, and the poor.

Key Fact

The Wagner Act (1935) guaranteed the right to organise trade unions and established the National Labor Relations Board to enforce those rights and investigate unfair employer practices. Trade union membership surged: the CIO (Congress of Industrial Organisations), a new federation for industrial workers, grew rapidly. The Social Security Act (1935) provided old-age pensions for workers over 65, funded by payroll taxes shared between employers and employees, and created a federal-state unemployment insurance system — the first federal safety net in American history.

After the Supreme Court struck down the NRA and AAA, Roosevelt proposed in February 1937 to appoint up to six additional justices — one for each sitting justice over 70. The plan was widely seen as an attempt to pack the Court with New Deal supporters and was defeated even in the Democrat-controlled Congress. The episode damaged Roosevelt’s political standing. Nevertheless, the Court’s composition changed naturally through retirement in 1937–39, and it became substantially more sympathetic to New Deal legislation without the packing plan ever being enacted.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on the New Deal often ask you to distinguish between the First and Second New Deals, or to explain the significance of individual agencies. Make sure you know which agencies were created in 1933 (AAA, CCC, FERA, NRA, TVA) and which came in 1935 (Wagner Act, Social Security Act, WPA). A common exam error is to describe the New Deal as a coherent, unified plan — it was improvised and contested. The NRA was declared unconstitutional in 1935, and even the Social Security Act excluded most African American workers from its coverage (domestic servants and farm labourers were left out). Including these limits raises your answer to the top band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Hundred Days (March–June 1933) created the First New Deal’s core agencies: AAA, CCC, FERA, NRA, and TVA — an unprecedented expansion of federal government intervention in the economy.
  • The Second New Deal (1935) shifted focus to workers’ rights and social security: the Wagner Act guaranteed collective bargaining, the Social Security Act created the first federal pension and unemployment system, and the WPA eventually employed over 8 million people.
  • The New Deal was politically contested throughout — the NRA was struck down by the Supreme Court in 1935, the court-packing plan failed in 1937, and many programmes excluded African American workers, showing the limits as well as the ambition of Roosevelt’s response.

lessons.title: Reactions to the New Deal
lessons.description: Critics on left and right, Supreme Court reversals and the New Deal's limits for Black Americans.
lessons.content_html:
The New Deal Contested

The New Deal was politically controversial from the moment it began. It faced sustained opposition from the political right and from business interests, but also significant criticism from the left — from those who argued it did not go far enough and actively excluded the poorest Americans. Understanding both types of opposition is essential for assessing the New Deal’s impact and limitations.

Key Fact

The main left-wing critics of the New Deal were Huey Long, who ran his “Share Our Wealth” clubs and threatened to challenge Roosevelt in 1936; Father Charles Coughlin, whose radio programme attracted millions of listeners; and Francis Townsend, who campaigned for a guaranteed pension for all Americans over 60. All three saw Roosevelt’s reforms as inadequate. The right-wing opposition was organised principally through the American Liberty League, founded by conservative Democrats and large corporations.

The Supreme Court Challenge

Between 1935 and 1936, the Supreme Court struck down several major New Deal programmes. The NRA was declared unconstitutional in Schechter Poultry v United States (May 1935) on the grounds that Congress had delegated too much legislative power to the executive branch. The AAA was struck down in United States v Butler (January 1936). These rulings threatened the entire edifice of the New Deal.

Roosevelt’s response — the court-packing plan of February 1937, proposing to add one new justice for each sitting justice over 70 — was rejected even by a Democrat-dominated Congress as an attack on judicial independence. Yet the court effectively backed down anyway, upholding the Wagner Act and Social Security Act in 1937. Historians often refer to this as “the switch in time that saved nine.” The court-packing episode demonstrated the limits of presidential authority and damaged Roosevelt’s reputation for pragmatic compromise.

Huey Long was one of the most colourful and dangerous political figures of the 1930s. As governor of Louisiana, he built roads, hospitals, and schools through a populist political machine that combined genuine reform with authoritarian methods. His “Share Our Wealth” plan proposed to cap personal fortunes at $3 million and use the revenue to guarantee every American family an annual income of at least $2,000. By 1935, the Share Our Wealth clubs had claimed over 7 million members. Political insiders feared Long might draw enough support from Roosevelt to throw the 1936 election to the Republicans. Long was assassinated in September 1935, removing this threat but also one of the New Deal’s most persistent critics.

The New Deal and African Americans

The New Deal’s relationship with African Americans was deeply contradictory. On one hand, more Black Americans benefited from federal programmes than ever before: the WPA employed hundreds of thousands, and Eleanor Roosevelt publicly championed civil rights, resigning from the Daughters of the American Revolution in 1939 when they refused to let Black singer Marian Anderson perform in their hall. Roosevelt appointed a group of African American advisers — informally called the Black Cabinet — headed by Mary McLeod Bethune.

Key Fact

Despite these gestures, the New Deal’s core programmes systematically excluded Black workers. The Social Security Act excluded domestic servants and agricultural labourers — the two occupations that employed the majority of Black Americans, especially in the South. The AAA’s production reduction payments went to landowners, while African American sharecroppers were displaced when landlords took land out of production rather than passing on benefits. The Federal Housing Administration’s mortgage guarantee programme institutionalised redlining, explicitly coding racial discrimination into federal housing policy.

Roosevelt’s decision in 1937 to cut federal spending sharply — under pressure from conservatives who argued the deficit was too large — plunged the economy back into recession. Unemployment, which had fallen from 25 per cent in 1932 to around 14 per cent by 1937, rose sharply again. Critics argued this demonstrated that the New Deal had not fixed the underlying economy — it had merely sustained demand through federal spending, and when that spending was cut, the recession returned. Roosevelt reversed course and increased spending again, but the political damage was done. The United States did not fully escape the Depression until wartime spending transformed the economy after 1941.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on reactions to the New Deal require balanced knowledge of right-wing, left-wing, and judicial opposition. A common mistake is to focus only on the Liberty League and ignore left-wing critics like Long, Coughlin, and Townsend. For the New Deal and African Americans, you must know specific examples of exclusion (Social Security excluding domestic servants and farm labourers; AAA displacing sharecroppers; FHA redlining) rather than just stating “the New Deal was racist.” Eleanor Roosevelt and the Black Cabinet show the positive dimension. The 1937 recession is important evidence that the New Deal had not permanently fixed the economy — use it in essays about the New Deal’s overall impact.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The New Deal faced opposition from the right (Liberty League, business interests), the left (Huey Long’s Share Our Wealth, Coughlin, Townsend), and the Supreme Court, which struck down the NRA and AAA in 1935–36.
  • The New Deal’s treatment of African Americans was contradictory: Eleanor Roosevelt and the Black Cabinet showed genuine engagement, but the Social Security Act excluded domestic servants and farm workers, the AAA displaced sharecroppers, and the FHA institutionalised redlining in federal housing policy.
  • The 1937 recession showed that the New Deal had not permanently fixed the economy — full recovery only came with wartime military spending after Pearl Harbor in 1941.

lessons.title: The Second World War and civil rights
lessons.description: Mobilisation, Japanese internment, Detroit riots and the wartime roots of civil rights.
lessons.content_html:
America Enters the War

On 7 December 1941, Japanese aircraft attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, killing around 2,400 Americans and destroying or damaging 19 naval vessels and over 300 aircraft. The following day, Congress declared war on Japan. Three days later, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. America’s long period of isolationism was over. The country mobilised with extraordinary speed and scale.

Key Fact

Wartime mobilisation saw a dramatic expansion of federal government power. The War Production Board co-ordinated industrial output, directing factories from car production to tanks and aircraft. By 1944, the United States was producing more war material than all the Axis powers combined. The federal workforce grew enormously. Taxation rose sharply to fund the war. Selective Service conscripted around 10 million Americans. And the government took unprecedented control of prices, wages, and allocation of materials through rationing and production quotas.

Women and the War Effort

With millions of men serving overseas, women entered the paid workforce in numbers never seen before. By 1944, over 19 million American women were in paid employment, including in industries previously considered exclusively male — shipyards, aircraft factories, and munitions plants. The iconic cultural figure of Rosie the Riveter, with the slogan “We Can Do It!” captured the wartime shift in gender roles.

However, the changes in women’s employment were presented as temporary contributions to the war effort, not permanent shifts in their status. After 1945, social pressure and government policy actively encouraged women to return to domestic roles to free jobs for returning veterans. Women in defence industries often faced lower pay than male counterparts doing identical work, and African American women faced compounded discrimination.

One of the most serious violations of civil liberties in American history occurred in February 1942, when Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, authorising the forced relocation of Japanese Americans from the West Coast. Approximately 120,000 people — around two-thirds of whom were American citizens born in the United States — were sent to internment camps in remote desert locations. Most lost their homes, businesses, and property. Fred Korematsu challenged his internment order in the courts; the Supreme Court upheld it in Korematsu v United States (1944), ruling that military necessity justified the measure. In 1988, President Ronald Reagan signed the Civil Liberties Act, issuing a formal apology and paying $20,000 in reparations to surviving internees.

Race on the Home Front

African Americans served in the armed forces in a segregated military, fighting for a democracy that denied them rights at home. Before the war had even begun, labour leader A. Philip Randolph, head of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, threatened to lead a March on Washington of 100,000 African Americans to demand an end to discrimination in defence industries. Roosevelt, alarmed by the prospect, signed Executive Order 8802 in June 1941, prohibiting racial discrimination in defence industries and federal agencies, and establishing a Fair Employment Practices Committee. It was the first presidential civil rights order since Reconstruction.

Key Fact

Executive Order 8802 was a landmark: it created the Fair Employment Practices Committee (FEPC) to investigate complaints of racial discrimination in war industries. However, the FEPC was underfunded and had no enforcement powers. Discrimination continued in practice, and the military itself remained rigidly segregated throughout the war. The order had been won through the threat of mass protest rather than spontaneous presidential generosity, establishing a model of political pressure that would characterise the civil rights movement for decades.

In June 1943, the Detroit Race Riot killed 34 people — 25 of them African American — over three days of violence. The riot arose from the extreme pressure on Detroit’s housing and employment from the massive wartime migration of both white and Black southerners to defence industry jobs. Federal troops were needed to restore order. Meanwhile, the all-Black Tuskegee Airmen flew combat missions over Europe, demonstrating African American capability and providing a powerful argument against military segregation. Their record of never losing a bomber to enemy fighters became a source of immense pride.

Truman and the Desegregation of the Military

Harry Truman, who became president after Roosevelt’s death in April 1945, took a more direct approach to racial equality than his predecessor. Influenced partly by reports of violence against returning Black veterans (who were beaten and even killed for wearing their uniforms in the South), Truman signed Executive Order 9981 in July 1948, ordering the desegregation of the US armed forces. It was a landmark civil rights act, though full implementation took years. The order is seen as a founding moment of the post-war civil rights movement.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This lesson has several specific facts that examiners test directly. Know the dates for key executive orders: EO 8802 (June 1941, fair employment), EO 9066 (February 1942, internment), EO 9981 (July 1948, military desegregation). Know A. Philip Randolph’s role — his threatened March on Washington forced EO 8802; the pattern of protest forcing action matters more than just the order itself. For Japanese internment, include both the injustice (two-thirds were US citizens) and the legal challenge (Korematsu 1944) as well as the eventual apology and reparations in 1988. Examiners reward students who can discuss both the limits and the significance of wartime changes for African Americans and women.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pearl Harbor (December 1941) brought the USA into the war; wartime mobilisation dramatically expanded federal power, employed millions of women in defence industries, and produced more war material than the Axis by 1944.
  • Executive Order 9066 (February 1942) interned approximately 120,000 Japanese Americans, most of them US citizens, in a constitutional violation formally apologised for by Reagan in 1988; A. Philip Randolph’s threatened March on Washington forced Roosevelt to sign Executive Order 8802 banning discrimination in defence industries.
  • The wartime experience — the Detroit Race Riot, the Tuskegee Airmen, the contradictions of Black soldiers fighting for democracy while denied rights at home — laid the foundations for the post-war civil rights movement; Truman’s Executive Order 9981 (July 1948) desegregated the military.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which the US federal government expanded its powers during the Second World War.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Each way scores 1 mark for identification and 1 additional mark for specific supporting detail. Example ways: conscription through Selective Service (1), which eventually drafted around 10 million Americans into the armed forces (1); the War Production Board directing industrial output (1), co-ordinating the shift from consumer goods to military production so that by 1944 the US was producing more war material than all Axis powers combined (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Japanese-American internment during the Second World War is considered a violation of civil liberties.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both reasons fully explained with specific evidence (e.g. around two-thirds of those interned were US citizens born in the United States — EO 9066 effectively punished people for their ethnic background rather than any proven disloyalty; the Supreme Court in Korematsu v United States upheld the internment in 1944 on grounds of military necessity, demonstrating that even constitutional protections could be suspended during wartime, a precedent considered deeply troubling by later jurists). Secure: Both reasons explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One explained well, one identified only. Emerging: One or both identified without causal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Executive Order 8802 was significant for the history of civil rights in the United States.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains significance in multiple dimensions — it was the first presidential civil rights executive order since Reconstruction; it was won through the threat of mass protest (A. Philip Randolph’s threatened March on Washington), establishing political pressure as a civil rights strategy; it created the FEPC; but also explains limits (FEPC underfunded, no enforcement, military remained segregated). Secure: Two or more dimensions explained with relevant evidence. Developing: One dimension explained, others named. Emerging: General statement without specific evidence.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Detroit Race Riot of 1943.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: The riot killed 34 people over three days of violence in June 1943 (1); 25 of the 34 dead were African American, reflecting the asymmetry of violence in which Black residents were disproportionately killed (1). Feature 2: Federal troops were required to restore order (1); the riot arose from extreme pressure on Detroit’s housing and employment caused by the wartime migration of both white and Black southerners to work in the city’s defence industries (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the Second World War was the foundation of the civil rights movement in the United States? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that acknowledges wartime foundations (EO 8802, Tuskegee Airmen, Double V campaign, Randolph’s March on Washington threat, contradictions of segregated military) while also recognising earlier roots (NAACP since 1909, Red Summer 1919, Garvey movement) and post-war continuity (Truman’s EO 9981, Brown v Board); engages with at least one interpretation. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both wartime and longer-term context. Developing: Some awareness of continuity and change. Emerging: Descriptive account without structured argument. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare the following two interpretations of women's wartime roles. Interpretation A argues the war permanently transformed women's status in American society. Interpretation B argues the changes were temporary and women were pushed back into domestic roles after 1945. How far do the interpretations differ, and what might explain their differences?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies key differences (permanence vs. temporariness of change, propaganda vs. reality); uses own knowledge to evaluate both (19 million women employed 1944, Rosie the Riveter imagery for A; post-war pressure to return home, lower pay than male counterparts, 1950s domestic ideology for B); explains why interpretations differ (contemporary vs. retrospective evidence, feminist vs. traditional perspective). Secure: Explains differences with relevant own knowledge. Developing: Identifies some differences and supports one. Emerging: Summarises each without explaining differences.
